metadata.title: A Global Geometric Framework for Nonlinear Dimensionality Reduction
metadata.authors: J. B. Tenenbaum, V. de Silva, J. C. Langford
metadata.source_note: Extracted from PDF->text fallback; .tex source not available. Math fidelity reduced (Greek letters and math symbols may be garbled in source; statements paraphrased conservatively from PDF text).

nodes.name: Nonlinear Dimensionality Reduction
nodes.statement: Given $N$ high-dimensional input vectors $x_i \in \mathbb{R}^D$ that lie on or near a low-dimensional nonlinear manifold $M$, recover coordinate vectors $y_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$ (with $d \ll D$) that capture the intrinsic geometry of the data.
nodes.statement_clean: Find low-dimensional coordinates that preserve the intrinsic geometry of high-dimensional data lying on a nonlinear manifold.

nodes.name: Geodesic (Manifold) Distance
nodes.statement: The geodesic distance $d_M(i,j)$ between points $i, j$ on a manifold $M$ is the length of the shortest path along $M$ connecting them.
nodes.statement_clean: Shortest-path distance measured along the manifold rather than through the ambient space.

nodes.name: Input-Space Distance
nodes.statement: The input-space distance $d_X(i,j)$ between data points $i, j$ is measured in the standard Euclidean metric (or a domain-specific metric such as tangent distance) in the ambient input space $X$.
nodes.statement_clean: Distance between two points as measured in the high-dimensional input space.

nodes.name: Neighborhood Graph $G$
nodes.statement: A weighted graph $G$ over the data points formed by connecting each point $i$ to all $j$ within $\epsilon$ ($\epsilon$-Isomap) or to its $K$ nearest neighbors ($K$-Isomap), with edge weight $d_X(i,j)$.
nodes.statement_clean: Graph where each point links to its local neighbors with edges weighted by input-space distance.

nodes.name: Graph (Shortest-Path) Distance $d_G$
nodes.statement: $d_G(i,j)$ is the shortest path distance from $i$ to $j$ in the neighborhood graph $G$, used as an estimate of the geodesic distance $d_M(i,j)$.
nodes.statement_clean: Shortest-path distance computed in the neighborhood graph, approximating the manifold geodesic.

nodes.name: Centering Operator $\tau$
nodes.statement: $\tau(D) = -H S H / 2$, where $S_{ij} = D_{ij}^2$ is the matrix of squared distances and $H_{ij} = \delta_{ij} - 1/N$ is the centering matrix; $\tau$ converts a distance matrix into the corresponding inner-product (Gram) matrix.
nodes.statement_clean: Operator that converts a squared-distance matrix into a centered Gram matrix used by classical MDS.

nodes.name: Residual Variance
nodes.statement: Residual variance $= 1 - R^2(\hat{D}_M, D_Y)$, where $\hat{D}_M$ is each algorithm's best estimate of intrinsic manifold distances ($D_G$ for Isomap, $D_X$ for PCA/MDS), $D_Y$ is the matrix of Euclidean distances in the recovered embedding, and $R$ is the linear correlation coefficient.
nodes.statement_clean: Goodness-of-fit measure: one minus the squared correlation between estimated manifold distances and embedding distances.

nodes.name: Isomap Cost Function (Eq. 1)
nodes.statement: $E = \| \tau(D_G) - \tau(D_Y) \|_{L^2}$, where $D_Y$ is the Euclidean distance matrix in the embedding $Y$ and $\| A \|_{L^2} = \sqrt{\sum_{i,j} A_{ij}^2}$.
nodes.statement_clean: Cost function minimized by Isomap: L2 difference between the centered Gram matrices of graph distances and embedding distances.

nodes.name: Graph-vs-Geodesic Distance Bound
nodes.statement: $(1 - \lambda_1) d_M(i,j) \leq d_G(i,j) \leq (1 + \lambda_2) d_M(i,j)$, holding uniformly over all pairs $i, j$ with probability at least $1 - \mu$.
nodes.statement_clean: Two-sided multiplicative bound showing graph distances closely approximate manifold geodesics.

nodes.name: Asymptotic Convergence of Isomap
nodes.statement: For data sampled from a manifold $M$ embedded in input space $X$, given arbitrarily small $\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \mu > 0$, one can choose neighborhood size $\epsilon$ (or $K$) and sample density $\alpha$ so that with probability $\geq 1 - \mu$, $(1-\lambda_1) d_M(i,j) \leq d_G(i,j) \leq (1+\lambda_2) d_M(i,j)$ uniformly over all pairs $i,j$.
nodes.statement_clean: As the number of data points increases, Isomap's graph distances converge to the true manifold geodesic distances with high probability.
assumptions: Data sampled from a manifold $M$ with minimal radius of curvature $r_0$ and minimal branch separation $s_0$
Neighborhood size satisfies $\epsilon \leq (2/\pi) r_0 \sqrt{24 \lambda_1}$ and $\epsilon < s_0$ (for $\epsilon$-Isomap)
$\alpha > [\log(V / \mu \eta_d (\lambda_2 \epsilon / 16)^d)] / \eta_d (\lambda_2 \epsilon / 8)^d$, where $V$ is the volume of $M$ and $\eta_d$ is the volume of the unit $d$-ball
conclusions: $(1-\lambda_1) d_M(i,j) \leq d_G(i,j) \leq (1+\lambda_2) d_M(i,j)$ uniformly over all $i,j$ with probability $\geq 1 - \mu$

nodes.name: Isomap
nodes.statement: Three-step nonlinear dimensionality-reduction algorithm: (1) build a neighborhood graph $G$ from input distances $d_X$; (2) approximate manifold geodesics $d_M(i,j)$ by graph shortest paths $d_G(i,j)$; (3) apply classical MDS to $D_G$ to embed in $\mathbb{R}^d$.
nodes.statement_clean: Build neighborhood graph, compute graph shortest paths, apply classical MDS to the resulting distance matrix.
output: Coordinate vectors $y_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$ that minimize the cost $E = \| \tau(D_G) - \tau(D_Y) \|_{L^2}$

nodes.name: Construct Neighborhood Graph
nodes.statement: Define graph $G$ over all data points by connecting $i, j$ if $d_X(i,j) < \epsilon$ ($\epsilon$-Isomap) or if $i$ is one of the $K$ nearest neighbors of $j$ ($K$-Isomap); set edge length to $d_X(i,j)$.

nodes.name: Compute Shortest Paths (Floyd's Algorithm)
nodes.statement: Initialize $d_G(i,j) = d_X(i,j)$ if linked, $\infty$ otherwise. For each $k = 1, 2, \ldots, N$, replace $d_G(i,j)$ by $\min\{ d_G(i,j),\, d_G(i,k) + d_G(k,j) \}$. Final $D_G = \{d_G(i,j)\}$ contains shortest-path distances.

nodes.name: Construct $d$-Dimensional Embedding via MDS
nodes.statement: Let $\lambda_p$ be the $p$-th eigenvalue (decreasing order) of $\tau(D_G)$ and $v_i^p$ the $i$-th component of the $p$-th eigenvector. Set the $p$-th coordinate of $y_i$ equal to $\sqrt{\lambda_p}\, v_i^p$.

nodes.name: Floyd's All-Pairs Shortest-Paths Algorithm
nodes.statement: Classical $O(N^3)$ dynamic-programming algorithm for computing all-pairs shortest path distances in a weighted graph; used in Isomap Step 2.
output: Matrix $D_G = \{ d_G(i,j) \}$ of all-pairs shortest path distances
nodes.origin_citation: Floyd's algorithm; see Kumar et al., Introduction to Parallel Computing (1994)

nodes.name: Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
nodes.statement: Linear dimensionality-reduction technique that finds a low-dimensional embedding of the data points that best preserves their variance as measured in the high-dimensional input space.
nodes.origin_citation: Classical (Pearson, Hotelling); cf. Mardia, Kent, Bibby 1979

nodes.name: Classical Multidimensional Scaling (MDS)
nodes.statement: Classical method that, given a distance matrix $D$, constructs a Euclidean embedding by computing the top eigenvectors of $\tau(D) = -H S H / 2$; equivalent to PCA when distances are Euclidean.

nodes.name: Swiss Roll Data Set
nodes.statement: Two-dimensional manifold embedded in $\mathbb{R}^3$ as a rolled sheet ($N=1000$ points): points far apart along the manifold appear close in Euclidean distance. Isomap with $K=7$ recovers the correct $d=2$ embedding; PCA and MDS fail.
nodes.statement_clean: Canonical synthetic 2D manifold embedded as a rolled surface in 3D, used to demonstrate Isomap.

nodes.name: Face Images under Pose and Lighting
nodes.statement: $N = 698$ synthetic $64 \times 64$ images of a face ($D = 4096$) varying in left-right pose, up-down pose, and lighting direction. Isomap ($K = 6$) recovers a $d=3$ embedding whose axes correlate strongly with the three known degrees of freedom ($R = 0.99, 0.90, 0.92$).
nodes.statement_clean: High-dimensional face image set with three known degrees of freedom; Isomap recovers them.

nodes.name: MNIST Handwritten 2's
nodes.statement: $N = 1000$ handwritten digit '2' images from MNIST, with input-space distances $d_X$ given by tangent distance. $\epsilon$-Isomap ($\epsilon = 4.2$) recovers an embedding whose two leading axes capture bottom-loop and top-arch articulation.
nodes.statement_clean: Handwritten digit example using tangent distance; Isomap discovers stylistic axes.

nodes.name: Hand Images (Finger Extension and Wrist Rotation)
nodes.statement: Set of noisy real images of a human hand varying in finger extension and wrist rotation; Isomap recovers the known low-dimensional structure.
nodes.statement_clean: Real hand-image data with known degrees of freedom recovered by Isomap.

nodes.name: Geodesic Interpolations along Isomap Coordinates
nodes.statement: Linear interpolations between distant points in the Isomap coordinate space induce perceptually natural but highly nonlinear 'morphs' of the corresponding high-dimensional images (faces, hands, handwritten 2's), approximately along geodesic paths on the manifold.
nodes.statement_clean: Straight lines in Isomap coordinates correspond to natural geodesic morphs in the original input space.

nodes.name: Sparse Shortest-Path Speedup
nodes.statement: Floyd's algorithm requires $O(N^3)$ operations; more efficient algorithms exploiting the sparse structure of the neighborhood graph (e.g., Dijkstra-based) can be used for large $N$.

nodes.name: Disconnected-Component Handling
nodes.statement: For finite data, $d_G(i,j)$ may fail to approximate $d_M(i,j)$ for points disconnected from the giant component of $G$; such outliers have infinite graph distances from the majority of points and can be deleted from analysis.

nodes.name: Generalization beyond Convex Euclidean Manifolds
nodes.statement: Asymptotic convergence (Theorem TP275.1) is established for manifolds whose intrinsic geometry is that of a convex region of Euclidean space. For non-Euclidean manifolds (sphere, torus), Isomap still produces a globally optimal low-dimensional Euclidean representation in the sense of minimizing Eq. 1, but the embedding is not isometric.

nodes.name: Comparison to Local Linear and Greedy Nonlinear Methods
nodes.statement: Local linear techniques (e.g., mixtures of local PCA) do not produce a single global coordinate system; greedy nonlinear methods (self-organizing maps, principal curves, autoencoders) discover global structure but lack guarantees of polynomial-time global optimality and asymptotic convergence that Isomap inherits from PCA/MDS.

edges.rationale: The notion of geodesic (manifold) distance defines what 'intrinsic geometry' means in the dimensionality-reduction problem.
Input-space distance $d_X$ is the input used to construct the neighborhood graph $G$.
Graph distance $d_G$ is defined as shortest path in the neighborhood graph $G$.
Step 1 constructs the neighborhood graph as defined.
Step 2 computes the graph distances $d_G$.
Step 3 applies the centering operator $\tau$ to $D_G$ before eigendecomposition.
The cost function is expressed in terms of $\tau(D_G)$ and $\tau(D_Y)$.
Step 2 of Isomap is Floyd's algorithm applied to the neighborhood graph.
Step 3 is classical MDS applied to the graph distance matrix $D_G$.
Isomap is defined as the algorithm that minimizes the cost function $E$.
The convergence theorem bounds the error between graph distance and geodesic distance.
The convergence theorem is stated in terms of $d_G$ approximating $d_M$.
The bound (Eq.) is the conclusion of the convergence theorem.
The asymptotic-convergence theorem provides the guarantee that justifies Isomap.
Isomap is the algorithm proposed to solve nonlinear dimensionality reduction.
PCA is a baseline (linear) approach to dimensionality reduction; cited for comparison.
Classical MDS is a baseline approach to dimensionality reduction; cited for comparison.
The Swiss roll experiment illustrates Isomap's recovery of nonlinear manifolds.
The face-image experiment illustrates Isomap on real high-dimensional data.
The MNIST '2's experiment illustrates $\epsilon$-Isomap with tangent distance.
The hand-image experiment illustrates Isomap on noisy real data.
Geodesic interpolation in Isomap coordinates illustrates the algorithm's perceptual coherence.
Residual variance is the metric used to evaluate Isomap on the Swiss roll (Fig. 2B).
Step 2 (shortest paths) operates on the neighborhood graph built in Step 1.
Step 3 (MDS embedding) operates on the distance matrix $D_G$ produced by Step 2.
